pos: n. (the designation of Joshaphat, one of David's valiant men)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Mithni, the Mithnite, a gentilic of unknown origin; no place called Mithen or Methen is named in Scripture; used once, 1 Chronicles 11:43.
biblical_def: Mithnite is a designation with no known home. It occurs once: “Hanan the son of Maachah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite” (1 Chronicles 11:43). The list it belongs to is the roll of David's valiant men, and it is one of the longer lists in Chronicles, running past the three and the thirty into a company of men identified chiefly by where they came from — the Baharumite, the Shaalbonite, the Hittite, the Ashterathite, the Aroerite, the Tizite, the Mahavite, the Moabite, the Mesobaite. The Chronicler's version extends well beyond the parallel in 2 Samuel 23, adding sixteen names that are found nowhere else in Scripture. Among them is Joshaphat, called the Mithnite after a town that has left no other trace. The chapter opens with the three who broke through the Philistine host to fetch David water from the well of Bethlehem, and ends with men like this one: unknown, unlocated, and listed by name in the word of God.

corruption_summary: A roll of soldiers is read as a relic of tribal honour culture; Chronicles keeps it because God keeps account of who stood with His anointed.
corruption_paragraphs: Long lists of warriors are easily dismissed as the self-congratulation of a military society. The Chronicler is doing something else with them. He is writing to a people with no army, no king and no independence, and he puts in front of them the names of every man who came to David when David had nothing. The list is an argument about loyalty, not about glory.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God records service rendered in obscurity. Joshaphat the Mithnite is named from a town nobody can find, in a list most readers skip, in a book written for exiles. That is three layers of obscurity, and his name is still in Scripture.

pos: n. (one of David's valiant men, called the Mithnite; a different man from Jehoshaphat king of Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Yoshaphat, the LORD judgeth, from shaphat, to judge, with the shortened divine name; named once in this English form, 1 Chronicles 11:43.
biblical_def: Joshaphat the Mithnite is one of David's valiant men: “Hanan the son of Maachah, and Joshaphat the Mithnite” (1 Chronicles 11:43). He is not Jehoshaphat the king of Judah, nor Jehoshaphat the recorder in David's cabinet, nor Jehoshaphat the son of Nimshi; the Authorized Version distinguishes him by the shorter spelling and by the gentilic attached to it. He belongs to the tail of the list in 1 Chronicles 11, the sixteen men the Chronicler adds beyond the roll in 2 Samuel. His name means the LORD judgeth, a confession that whatever a man's standing before the world, the sentence that matters is pronounced elsewhere. The company he is numbered in had come to David in the wilderness, when the throne was Saul's and the anointing was David's, and every man in the list had to decide which of those two facts governed.

corruption_summary: Shared names are flattened into one figure; the Authorized Version keeps the spellings distinct and so does any honest reference work.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture has several Jehoshaphats and one Joshaphat, and a careless reader merges them. The distinction matters for the same reason every distinction in a genealogy matters: the men were different men, and a dictionary that confuses them has made the record say what it does not say. This entry is for the Mithnite among David's valiant men and for nobody else.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is exactness in handling the text, which is a species of reverence. The name he bore is a true sentence whichever man carried it: “But God is the judge: he putteth down one, and setteth up another” (Psalm 75:7).

pos: n. (the designation of Joha, brother of Jediael, among David's valiant men)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Titsi, the Tizite, a gentilic of unknown origin; no place of that name occurs elsewhere; used once, 1 Chronicles 11:45.
biblical_def: Tizite is another of the unplaceable designations in David's roll: “Jediael the son of Shimri, and Joha his brother, the Tizite” (1 Chronicles 11:45). Two brothers appear together, which is unusual in the list and worth noting; most of the valiant men are given singly. The Authorized Version's margin at this verse notes an alternative reading of the patronymic, which is characteristic of these later names in Chronicles, where the Hebrew is at its most difficult and the translators recorded the variants rather than choosing silently. Nothing is known of Tiz, and nothing further is told of Joha. He stands in the company of men who, in the words of the chapter's opening, came to David at Hebron and “strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel” (1 Chronicles 11:10).

corruption_summary: Brothers serving side by side is treated as incidental; Chronicles records it, because households as well as individuals came over to the anointed king.
corruption_paragraphs: The roll of the valiant men is mostly a list of single men with single towns. Jediael and Joha are listed as brothers, and the detail is preserved. The chapter is about a kingdom gathering itself around God's choice, and it gathered by families as well as by individuals — Joab and Abishai and Asahel, Jediael and Joha.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God ordinarily works along the lines of the households He created. “So David waxed greater and greater: for the LORD of hosts was with him” (1 Chronicles 11:9). The growth came man by man and brother by brother, and the record keeps both.

pos: n. (the designation of Eliahba, one of David's thirty, from Shaalbon or Shaalbim)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Sha'alvoni, the Shaalbonite, from Shaalbon, generally identified with Shaalbim, a place of foxes or jackals; used twice, 2 Samuel 23:32 and 1 Chronicles 11:33.
biblical_def: Shaalbonite is the designation of one of David's thirty, and it occurs in both parallel rolls: “Eliahba the Shaalbonite, of the sons of Jashen, Jonathan” (2 Samuel 23:32), and “Azmaveth the Baharumite, Eliahba the Shaalbonite” (1 Chronicles 11:33). Shaalbon is generally taken for Shaalbim, a town in the territory allotted to Dan which the Danites could not clear: the Amorites “would dwell in mount Heres in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim” (Judges 1:35) until the house of Joseph prevailed over them. The name appears to mean a place of foxes. If the identification holds, Eliahba came from a town Israel had taken late and with difficulty, in a tribal inheritance that was never properly possessed, and he ended among the thirty men whose names were written down because of what they did for David.

corruption_summary: A man is assumed to be limited by the failure of his tribe; Dan never cleared its inheritance, and a man of one of its contested towns stood among David's thirty.
corruption_paragraphs: Dan is the tribe that could not take its allotment and ended up migrating north, and Judges records the Amorites forcing the Danites into the mountain. Shaalbim was one of the towns in dispute. The sons of a tribe that failed are not thereby condemned to fail, and Eliahba the Shaalbonite is in the roll of the thirty.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's dealings are with persons as well as peoples, and a faithful man may stand inside an unfaithful inheritance. The same chapter that names him names Uriah the Hittite — a foreigner among the thirty, more loyal to the ark than the king who killed him.

pos: n. (the Philistine of Timnath whose daughter Samson married)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Timni, the Timnite, a gentilic from Timnath, a portion or allotted place; used once, Judges 15:6.
biblical_def: The Timnite is the father of Samson's first wife, and he is named only as the Philistines are about to burn him: “Then the Philistines said, Who hath done this? And they answered, Samson, the son in law of the Timnite, because he had taken his wife, and given her to his companion. And the Philistines came up, and burnt her and her father with fire” (Judges 15:6). The chain of events runs back to Samson's insistence on the marriage against his parents' objection, through the riddle at the feast, the threat that extracted its answer, the giving away of the bride, and then the three hundred foxes: “And when he had set the brands on fire, he let them go into the standing corn of the Philistines, and burnt up both the shocks, and also the standing corn, with the vineyards and olives” (Judges 15:5). The Philistines answered the burning of their harvest by burning the woman they had earlier threatened to burn, and her father with her. Everything in the account is lawless, and the narrator has already told us what God was doing in it.

corruption_summary: A violent chapter is read as evidence against Scripture's morality; the narrator passes no approval on any of it and tells us plainly what God was doing through it.
corruption_paragraphs: Judges 14 and 15 are an unrelieved record of lust, deceit, extortion, arson and murder, and Samson is not exempted from the charge. Scripture reports it without commendation. What it does supply is the governing fact, stated before the trouble begins: “But his father and his mother knew not that it was of the LORD, that he sought an occasion against the Philistines: for at that time the Philistines had dominion over Israel” (Judges 14:4).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the distinction between God's decree and God's precept. The LORD governed the whole affair toward the deliverance of Israel; He did not approve one sinful act within it. The Timnite is burnt by his own people for a quarrel he did not begin, and the book of Judges does not soften the horror of it.

pos: n. (the people and territory of Maachah, on the border of Bashan, never dispossessed by Israel)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Ma'akhathi, the Maachathite, from Maachah, oppression or pressure; used once in this form, Deuteronomy 3:14.
biblical_def: Maachathi names a small Aramean kingdom on the northeastern frontier of Israel's inheritance: “Jair the son of Manasseh took all the country of Argob unto the coasts of Geshuri and Maachathi; and called them after his own name, Bashanhavothjair, unto this day” (Deuteronomy 3:14). The context is the conquest of Og: “And the rest of Gilead, and all Bashan, being the kingdom of Og, gave I unto the half tribe of Manasseh; all the region of Argob, with all Bashan, which was called the land of giants” (Deuteronomy 3:13). Israel took Argob up to the border of Geshur and Maachah, and stopped there. Joshua records the consequence plainly: the children of Israel “expelled not the Geshurites, nor the Maachathites: but the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day” (Joshua 13:13). Centuries later, David's son Absalom fled to Geshur, where his mother's father was king, and a Maachathite mercenary army fought against David at Helam.

corruption_summary: An unfinished obedience is read as pragmatism; the nations Israel left in place became, generation after generation, exactly the snare God had warned of.
corruption_paragraphs: Israel took Bashan and stopped at the border of Geshur and Maachah, and the omission is recorded without comment in Deuteronomy and with a plain note of failure in Joshua: the Geshurites and the Maachathites dwell among the Israelites until this day. It looked harmless. It was from Geshur that David took a wife whose son Absalom murdered his brother, fled to his grandfather's court, and later raised rebellion against his father.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that partial obedience is disobedience with a delayed account. The LORD had said what the remaining nations would be: pricks in the eyes and thorns in the sides. Maachah is one of the thorns, and the book of Samuel is where the wound appears.

pos: n. (one of the eleven Canaanite peoples descended from Canaan the son of Ham)
etymology: Hebrew ha-Tsemari, the Zemarite, from a root signifying wool or a fleece; generally connected with the Phoenician town of Simyra; named twice, Genesis 10:18 and 1 Chronicles 1:16.
biblical_def: The Zemarite is one of the peoples in the table of nations: “And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite: and afterward were the families of the Canaanites spread abroad” (Genesis 10:18), repeated in the Chronicler's compressed version, “And the Arvadite, and the Zemarite, and the Hamathite” (1 Chronicles 1:16). Canaan's descendants are given in order from Sidon the firstborn southward and inland — “And Canaan begat Sidon his firstborn, and Heth” (Genesis 10:15) — and the last three named, Arvad, Zemar and Hamath, are northern, in what later ages called Phoenicia and Syria. The Zemarites are generally identified with the town of Simyra on that coast. They appear nowhere else in Scripture; unlike the Hittites, Jebusites and Amorites, they never meet Israel in the narrative. Genesis 10 is the Bible's claim that every nation on earth descends from one family off one ark, and it names peoples who have no further part in the story precisely to make that claim complete.

corruption_summary: The table of nations is treated as ancient ethnography; it is Scripture's claim that mankind is one family, which no later theory of races can overturn.
corruption_paragraphs: Genesis 10 lists seventy nations, several of which — the Zemarite among them — never appear again. The completeness is deliberate. The chapter exists to establish that every people on the earth came of the three sons of Noah, and therefore of Adam, and that there is no second origin for any branch of mankind.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the biblical doctrine of one human race. Paul states it to the philosophers at Athens: God “hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Acts 17:26). The Zemarites are in the Bible to make the list whole.

pos: n. (the father of On the Reubenite in Korah's rebellion; also a son of Jonathan of the house of Jerahmeel)
etymology: Hebrew Peleth, swiftness, or flight, from palat or a kindred root signifying escape; named at Numbers 16:1 and 1 Chronicles 2:33.
biblical_def: Two men bear the name, and the first is remembered for his son's one appearance in a rebellion. “Now Korah, the son of Izhar, the son of Kohath, the son of Levi, and Dathan and Abiram, the sons of Eliab, and On, the son of Peleth, sons of Reuben, took men” (Numbers 16:1). On the son of Peleth is named as one of the ringleaders and then never mentioned again — not in the confrontation, not among those who stood at their tent doors, not in the roll of the swallowed. Whether he withdrew, Scripture does not say; it simply stops naming him, and when the earth opened it took “the men that appertained unto Korah, and all their goods” (Numbers 16:32). The second Peleth is in the Jerahmeelite genealogy: “And the sons of Jonathan; Peleth, and Zaza. These were the sons of Jerahmeel” (1 Chronicles 2:33). The name means flight or escape, which the first man's son may have made.

corruption_summary: Rebellion is framed as a demand for equal access to holy things; Korah's company claimed the whole congregation was holy and were swallowed for it.
corruption_paragraphs: The argument Korah made sounds unimpeachable in modern ears: all the congregation are holy, every one of them, so why lift yourselves above the assembly. Two hundred and fifty princes of the assembly, famous in the congregation, men of renown (Numbers 16:2) found it persuasive. The LORD answered it by opening the ground.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God appoints to office, and that the levelling of what He has distinguished is not humility but revolt. On the son of Peleth is named at the start and absent at the end, which is the one faint mercy in the chapter. Whoever leaves such a company leaves it before the ground moves.

pos: n. (one of the five kings of Midian slain by Israel, called a duke of Sihon)
etymology: Hebrew Reva, a fourth part, or offspring, from arba, four, or a kindred root; named twice, Numbers 31:8 and Joshua 13:21.
biblical_def: Reba is fifth in a list of five kings: “And they slew the kings of Midian, beside the rest of them that were slain; namely, Evi, and Rekem, and Zur, and Hur, and Reba, five kings of Midian: Balaam also the son of Beor they slew with the sword” (Numbers 31:8). Joshua repeats the roll and adds their political standing: the same five are “princes of Midian, Evi, and Rekem, and Zur, and Hur, and Reba, which were dukes of Sihon, dwelling in the country” (Joshua 13:21). They were vassals of the Amorite king whose kingdom Israel had already taken. The war against Midian was commanded because of Peor — the counsel of Balaam, by which Midianite women drew Israel into idolatry and whoredom, and twenty-four thousand died of the plague. “And they warred against the Midianites, as the LORD commanded Moses; and they slew all the males” (Numbers 31:7). Balaam, who had taken Balak's fee and given the advice, died with the kings he had served.

corruption_summary: The Midianite war is cited as naked aggression; Scripture ties it directly to Peor, where Midian's counsel destroyed twenty-four thousand Israelites.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 31 is read as an atrocity out of context, and context is exactly what the surrounding chapters supply. Midian had not been attacked; Midian had, on Balaam's advice, deliberately used its women to draw Israel into the worship of Baal-peor, and a plague had killed twenty-four thousand. The war is judicial, declared by God, bounded by His command, and executed on the men who devised it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God is a just judge who punishes nations for specific, named crimes, and that the record names them. “Balaam also the son of Beor, the soothsayer, did the children of Israel slay with the sword among them that were slain by them” (Joshua 13:22). The man who sold the counsel died beside the kings who bought it.

pos: n. (a son of Jeroham, a head of the fathers in Benjamin dwelling at Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Shamsheray, sun-like, or heroic, apparently from shemesh, the sun; named once, 1 Chronicles 8:26.
biblical_def: Shamsherai appears in the Benjamite register: “And Shamsherai, and Shehariah, and Athaliah” (1 Chronicles 8:26). The names around him belong to the sons of Jeroham and of Shashak — “And Iphedeiah, and Penuel, the sons of Shashak” (1 Chronicles 8:25) — and the whole block is summed up two verses on: “These were heads of the fathers, by their generations, chief men. These dwelt in Jerusalem” (1 Chronicles 8:28). The chapter is Benjamin's own roll, set just before the Chronicler turns to the men who dwelt in Jerusalem after the captivity, and it runs down to the house of Saul. His name appears to be built on shemesh, the sun, a word Israel used freely in place-names and personal names although the sun itself was a god to every nation around them. Scripture will use the creature's name without fearing the creature.

corruption_summary: The use of a pagan word in a godly name is read as syncretism; Israel used the names of created things freely, because the creature is not a rival to its Maker.
corruption_paragraphs: Every nation around Israel worshipped the sun, and Israel named towns and men with the word for it — Beth-shemesh, En-shemesh, Samson, and this man of Benjamin. The usage is not a concession. Scripture treats the sun as a lamp God hung in the firmament on the fourth day, and nothing more, and so can name a child after it without apology.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the thorough de-divinising of nature that runs through the whole Bible. “For the LORD God is a sun and shield: the LORD will give grace and glory” (Psalm 84:11). The creature may be used as a figure of the Creator precisely because it is not a god.
